topics.name: Lobes & brainstem
topics.intro: The cerebrum is divided into frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital lobes, with the insula hidden deep in the Sylvian fissure. Below the tentorium sit the brainstem (midbrain, pons, medulla) and cerebellum. Scroll through the axial CT and watch the coloured slice and the 3D cut move together. Remember CT is displayed radiologically: the patient's left is on the right of the screen.

topics.name: CSF system
topics.intro: CSF is made mainly by choroid plexus in the lateral ventricles and flows: lateral ventricles → foramina of Monro → third ventricle → cerebral aqueduct → fourth ventricle → foramina of Luschka and Magendie → basal cisterns → subarachnoid space over the convexities → arachnoid granulations into the venous sinuses. On an ICU CT check three things every time: ventricle size (hydrocephalus?), the basal cisterns (open or effaced?), and blood in the ventricles or cisterns. Scroll from the vertex down to the foramen magnum and follow the flow.

topics.name: Fissures & sulci
topics.intro: Fissures and sulci are the landmarks that let you name the lobes on a CT slice. The interhemispheric fissure divides the hemispheres; the Sylvian fissure separates the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes; the central sulcus divides frontal from parietal; on the medial surface the parieto-occipital sulcus separates parietal from occipital, and the calcarine sulcus lies within the occipital lobe. Sulcal effacement (sulci disappearing) is an early sign of brain swelling.

topics.name: Falx & tentorium
topics.intro: The dura forms two rigid sheets that divide the cranial cavity: the falx cerebri between the hemispheres and the tentorium cerebelli between the cerebrum and cerebellum. Because the skull and these folds cannot stretch, a mass pushes brain past their free edges — herniation. Supratentorial masses herniate under the falx (subfalcine) or down through the tentorial notch (uncal/central); posterior fossa masses push up through the notch or down through the foramen magnum. Try the coronal view, and the 3D model with the lobes hidden.

structures.name: Frontal lobe
structures.notes: Anterior to the central sulcus and above the Sylvian fissure. Contains motor cortex (precentral gyrus), Broca's area (dominant inferior frontal gyrus), and prefrontal cortex for executive function and behaviour. The orbitofrontal surfaces sit on the anterior cranial fossa roof — a classic site for contusions after deceleration injury.
structures.ctNotes: Look along the orbital roofs and frontal poles for contre-coup contusions; they are easily missed adjacent to bone — use a narrow window.

structures.name: Parietal lobe
structures.notes: Behind the central sulcus, in front of the parieto-occipital sulcus. Primary somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus) and association cortex for spatial awareness. Non-dominant parietal lesions cause neglect — a useful bedside sign in the sedation hold.
structures.ctNotes: On high axial slices the central sulcus separates frontal from parietal; the precentral gyrus is usually thicker than the postcentral.

structures.name: Temporal lobe
structures.notes: Below the Sylvian fissure in the middle cranial fossa. Auditory cortex, Wernicke's area (dominant superior temporal gyrus) and memory structures medially. The medial temporal lobe (uncus, parahippocampal gyrus) lies at the tentorial edge and herniates over it in uncal herniation, compressing CN III and the midbrain.
structures.ctNotes: Temporal poles sit against the greater wing of sphenoid — another contusion site. Beam-hardening artefact from the petrous bones can mimic or hide pathology here.

structures.name: Occipital lobe
structures.notes: Posterior to the parieto-occipital sulcus, above the tentorium. Primary visual cortex lines the calcarine sulcus. Supplied mainly by the posterior cerebral artery — PCA compression against the tentorium in transtentorial herniation can cause occipital infarction.
structures.ctNotes: Look for the calcarine sulcus on medial axial slices just above the tentorium.

structures.name: Insula
structures.notes: Cortex buried deep in the Sylvian fissure, covered by the frontal, parietal and temporal opercula. Supplied by MCA branches running over its surface.
structures.ctNotes: Loss of the insular ribbon (insula blending with the adjacent white matter / extreme capsule) is one of the earliest CT signs of MCA infarction and is an ASPECTS region.

structures.name: Cingulate / limbic cortex
structures.notes: The cingulate gyrus wraps around the corpus callosum on the medial surface of each hemisphere, beneath the falx. In subfalcine herniation the cingulate gyrus is pushed under the free edge of the falx, and the anterior cerebral arteries can be compressed.
structures.ctNotes: Midline shift is measured at the septum pellucidum, just below the cingulate gyri.

structures.name: Corpus callosum
structures.notes: The largest commissure, joining the two hemispheres: rostrum and genu in front, body over the lateral ventricles, splenium behind. It forms the roof of the lateral ventricles and lies directly beneath the falx and cingulate gyri. The splenium and body are classic sites of diffuse axonal injury after high-energy trauma.
structures.ctNotes: Small haemorrhages in the corpus callosum (especially the splenium) on CT after trauma suggest diffuse axonal injury, which is often far worse on MRI. CT can look nearly normal despite deep coma.

structures.name: Internal capsule
structures.notes: A compact V-shaped band of white matter (apex medially, the genu) between the caudate and thalamus medially and the lentiform nucleus laterally. The posterior limb carries the corticospinal tract, so a small lacunar infarct or haemorrhage here can cause a dense contralateral hemiplegia. Supplied mainly by lenticulostriate arteries (MCA) and the anterior choroidal artery.
structures.ctNotes: On axial CT at the level of the third ventricle, look for the '>' / '<' shape of each internal capsule; ASPECTS region IC. Putaminal haemorrhages often extend into it.

structures.name: Cerebellum
structures.notes: Occupies most of the posterior fossa beneath the tentorium. Coordinates movement — lesions cause ipsilateral ataxia. The posterior fossa is a small, rigid compartment: cerebellar swelling or haemorrhage can rapidly compress the fourth ventricle (obstructive hydrocephalus) and the brainstem, and push the tonsils through the foramen magnum.
structures.ctNotes: Posterior fossa CT is degraded by beam hardening between the petrous bones. Check the fourth ventricle is open and the temporal horns are not dilated.

structures.name: Midbrain
structures.notes: Uppermost brainstem, passing through the tentorial notch. Contains the CN III and IV nuclei, the cerebral peduncles (corticospinal tracts) and the aqueduct. Compression in transtentorial herniation produces a fixed dilated pupil, reduced conscious level and posturing; Duret haemorrhages may follow.
structures.ctNotes: On axial CT the midbrain has a 'Mickey Mouse' shape surrounded by the ambient and quadrigeminal cisterns. Effacement of these cisterns is a key sign of raised ICP.

structures.name: Pons
structures.notes: Middle brainstem, anterior to the fourth ventricle, resting on the clivus. Contains CN V–VIII nuclei and the corticospinal tracts. The basilar artery runs in the prepontine cistern in front of it — basilar occlusion is an important cause of coma with an initially near-normal CT.
structures.ctNotes: A hyperdense basilar artery in the prepontine cistern can be the only CT clue to basilar thrombosis.

structures.name: Medulla
structures.notes: Lowest brainstem, continuous with the spinal cord at the foramen magnum. Contains the cardiorespiratory centres and CN IX–XII nuclei. Tonsillar herniation compresses the medulla, causing Cushing's response, respiratory arrest and death.
structures.ctNotes: At the foramen magnum, the cerebellar tonsils should not crowd out the CSF around the medulla (cisterna magna).

structures.name: Caudate nucleus
structures.notes: C-shaped nucleus whose head forms the lateral wall of the frontal horn of the lateral ventricle. Part of the basal ganglia. Supplied by lenticulostriate arteries and the recurrent artery of Heubner.
structures.ctNotes: The caudate head is an ASPECTS region (C). Caudate atrophy enlarges the frontal horns.

structures.name: Lentiform nucleus
structures.notes: Putamen (lateral) and globus pallidus (medial), separated from the caudate and thalamus by the internal capsule. The putamen is the commonest site of hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage. The globus pallidus is classically affected in carbon monoxide poisoning and hypoxic injury.
structures.ctNotes: Loss of the clear outline of the lentiform nucleus is an early sign of MCA (lenticulostriate) infarction — ASPECTS region L.

structures.name: Thalamus
structures.notes: Paired relay nuclei either side of the third ventricle, medial to the posterior limb of the internal capsule. Second commonest site of hypertensive haemorrhage; thalamic bleeds often rupture into the ventricles (IVH → hydrocephalus). Bilateral thalamic infarction (artery of Percheron, deep venous thrombosis) causes coma.
structures.ctNotes: Bilateral thalamic hypodensity should prompt a look at the deep veins and straight sinus for thrombosis.

structures.name: Hippocampus
structures.notes: Medial temporal grey matter in the floor of the temporal horn, essential for memory. Very sensitive to hypoxia and prolonged seizures.
structures.ctNotes: Poorly seen on CT; dilated temporal horns next to it are an early sign of hydrocephalus.

structures.name: Amygdala
structures.notes: Nuclear complex in the anteromedial temporal lobe, in front of the hippocampus and deep to the uncus. Marks the region that herniates medially over the tentorial edge in uncal herniation.

structures.name: Lateral ventricle
structures.notes: Paired C-shaped cavities: frontal horn, body, atrium (trigone), occipital horn and temporal horn. Each drains through its foramen of Monro into the third ventricle. Choroid plexus in the atrium often calcifies. EVDs are aimed at the frontal horn just anterior to the foramen of Monro.
structures.ctNotes: Early hydrocephalus: rounded frontal horns and temporal horns wider than ~2 mm. Midline shift: measure the septum pellucidum's displacement from the midline.

structures.name: Third ventricle
structures.notes: Slit-like midline cavity between the two thalami. Receives CSF from both lateral ventricles through the foramina of Monro and drains through the cerebral aqueduct. Its floor (hypothalamus, mammillary bodies) is opened in endoscopic third ventriculostomy.
structures.ctNotes: Normally a thin slit. A rounded, ballooned third ventricle suggests obstruction at or below the aqueduct. A colloid cyst at the foramina of Monro can cause sudden obstructive hydrocephalus.

structures.name: Cerebral aqueduct
structures.notes: Narrow channel (about 1–2 mm) through the midbrain joining the third and fourth ventricles. The narrowest point of the ventricular system, so it blocks easily: aqueduct stenosis, tectal tumours, or clot from intraventricular haemorrhage.
structures.ctNotes: Seen as a dot of CSF in the midbrain behind the cerebral peduncles. Dilated lateral and third ventricles with a normal fourth ventricle point to an aqueduct block.

structures.name: Fourth ventricle
structures.notes: Tent-shaped cavity between the pons/medulla in front and the cerebellum behind. Drains through the midline foramen of Magendie and paired lateral foramina of Luschka into the cisterna magna and cerebellopontine angles.
structures.ctNotes: Should be an open midline 'horseshoe' shape. Effacement or displacement from a cerebellar mass, infarct or haemorrhage is a neurosurgical emergency: risk of obstructive hydrocephalus and brainstem compression.

structures.name: Suprasellar cistern
structures.notes: Star- or pentagon-shaped CSF space above the pituitary fossa containing the optic chiasm, pituitary stalk and the circle of Willis. The commonest place to see blood in aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage.
structures.ctNotes: Look for the five- or six-pointed star on axial slices at the level of the midbrain. Hyperdense blood filling it means SAH; loss of the star (effacement) is a sign of raised ICP or uncal herniation.

structures.name: Interpeduncular cistern
structures.notes: Small CSF space between the cerebral peduncles at the front of the midbrain, behind the suprasellar cistern. Contains the basilar tip and the origins of CN III.
structures.ctNotes: A small dependent pocket where a little subarachnoid blood can collect — always check it, especially in subtle or late-presenting SAH.

structures.name: Ambient cistern
structures.notes: Thin CSF wings wrapping around the sides of the midbrain, linking the interpeduncular cistern in front to the quadrigeminal cistern behind. Contain the PCA, superior cerebellar artery and basal vein.
structures.ctNotes: With the quadrigeminal cistern these form the perimesencephalic cisterns. Asymmetric narrowing suggests uncal herniation on that side; complete effacement suggests severe raised ICP. Blood confined here may be non-aneurysmal perimesencephalic SAH.

structures.name: Quadrigeminal cistern
structures.notes: CSF space behind the midbrain tectum (colliculi), beneath the splenium of the corpus callosum. Contains the vein of Galen; the pineal gland sits at its front.
structures.ctNotes: Forms the 'smile' behind the midbrain on axial CT. Loss of the smile is a key raised-ICP / downward herniation sign. A common site for layering IVH or SAH.

structures.name: Prepontine cistern
structures.notes: CSF space between the clivus and the front of the pons, containing the basilar artery and CN VI.
structures.ctNotes: Look for a hyperdense basilar artery (thrombosis) or blood here. Effacement occurs with posterior fossa mass effect.

structures.name: Cisterna magna
structures.notes: Largest cistern, behind the medulla and below the cerebellum, just above the foramen magnum. Receives CSF from the fourth ventricle via the foramen of Magendie.
structures.ctNotes: Effacement, with the cerebellar tonsils crowding the foramen magnum, is the CT clue to tonsillar herniation. Its size varies a lot between people (a large one is usually normal).

structures.name: Interhemispheric fissure
structures.notes: Deep midline cleft (longitudinal fissure) separating the two cerebral hemispheres, occupied by the falx cerebri. Below the falx's free edge the hemispheres are joined by the corpus callosum.
structures.ctNotes: Judge midline shift against the fissure and falx. A dense falx with blood tracking along it suggests an interhemispheric subdural haematoma; blood within the anterior fissure suggests anterior communicating artery aneurysm SAH.

structures.name: Sylvian (lateral) fissure
structures.notes: Deep fissure separating the temporal lobe below from the frontal and parietal lobes above, with the insula at its depth. The MCA and its branches run through it.
structures.ctNotes: Effacement of one Sylvian fissure is an early sign of swelling (e.g. MCA infarct). Blood here suggests MCA aneurysm SAH. Widened fissures are seen with atrophy.

structures.name: Central sulcus
structures.notes: Separates the frontal lobe (precentral gyrus — primary motor cortex) from the parietal lobe (postcentral gyrus — primary sensory cortex). Runs from the vertex downwards and forwards, almost reaching the Sylvian fissure.
structures.ctNotes: On high axial slices, find the superior frontal sulcus running front-to-back; it ends by meeting the precentral sulcus at a right angle. The central sulcus is the next sulcus behind that. The precentral gyrus is thicker than the postcentral, and the 'hand knob' (an omega-shaped bulge of precentral gyrus) points backwards into it.

structures.name: Parieto-occipital sulcus
structures.notes: Deep sulcus on the medial surface separating the parietal lobe (precuneus) from the occipital lobe (cuneus). Joins the calcarine sulcus to form a 'Y' on a midline sagittal view.
structures.ctNotes: Best seen on sagittal reformats; on axial slices it runs obliquely backwards on the medial surface, marking the parietal–occipital boundary.

structures.name: Calcarine sulcus
structures.notes: Horizontal sulcus on the medial occipital lobe, lined by primary visual cortex. The upper bank represents the lower visual field and vice versa.
structures.ctNotes: Occipital (PCA) infarction involving the calcarine cortex causes a contralateral homonymous hemianopia — easily missed in a sedated patient.

structures.name: Falx cerebri
structures.notes: Sickle-shaped fold of dura in the interhemispheric fissure, from the crista galli in front to the tentorium behind. Its attached upper border carries the superior sagittal sinus and its free lower edge the inferior sagittal sinus. It joins the tentorium along the straight sinus.
structures.ctNotes: Normally faintly dense and often calcified with age (not blood). Subfalcine herniation: the cingulate gyrus slides under the free edge, displacing the septum pellucidum; measure midline shift at the foramina of Monro. A thickened, dense falx may be an interhemispheric subdural.

structures.name: Tentorium cerebelli
structures.notes: Tent-shaped fold of dura roofing the posterior fossa, separating the occipital and temporal lobes above (supratentorial) from the cerebellum below (infratentorial). Its free medial edge bounds the tentorial notch (incisura), through which the midbrain passes. The transverse sinuses run in its attached edge and the straight sinus where it meets the falx.
structures.ctNotes: The supra/infratentorial division underpins herniation: uncal and central (transtentorial) herniation down through the notch, and upward herniation from posterior fossa masses. Subdural blood along the tentorium appears as a dense sloping band on axial slices and is clearer on coronal reformats.
